title: Closing of density wake in concentrated colloidal suspensions: two regimes governed by compressibility, friction, and self-propulsion
authors: Guillaume Duprez, Gianmarco Spera, Benjamin Buhl, François Graner, Vincent Démery, Cécile Cottin-Bizonne, Hélène Delanoë-Ayari, Mathieu Leocmach
abstract: When an obstacle moves through a compressible medium, it creates a density perturbation. Theoretical arguments regarding the shape of this density wake in Brownian suspensions either suppose infinite dilution or describe only the far field. Here, we study via experiments and numerical simulations the closing of the density perturbation just behind a circular obstacle in dense 2D suspensions of particles that are thermal or self-propelled. In the thermal case, we show that the characteristic length of the wake is a non-monotonic function of density, decreasing then increasing. We rationalise the scalings of both regimes by analytical arguments that highlight the role of the compressibility factor of the suspension. Based on this new understanding of the passive case, we show that the influence of self-propulsion observed in experiments and simulations can be understood as if the obstacle is effectively larger in an active bath, with non-trivial and distinct roles of the self-propulsion velocity and of the persistence time.
summary: This work experimentally and numerically investigates how a density wake closes behind a moving object in dense colloidal suspensions. It establishes that the wake dynamics are fundamentally controlled by the suspension's compressibility, revealing distinct scaling laws for passive and active matter. The findings provide a framework to interpret the complex effects of self-propulsion in dense, non-equilibrium particle systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the closing of the density wake created when an obstacle moves through a dense, compressible colloidal suspension, addressing limitations of previous dilute or far-field theories.
main_result: The wake closing exhibits two distinct regimes governed by compressibility, and the influence of self-propulsion can be understood as an effective increase in the obstacle size within an active bath.
method: The research combines experimental measurements using Janus colloids with numerical simulations and analytical derivations based on continuum models.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D suspension of colloidal particles, which can be modeled as thermal (passive) or self-propelled (active) Brownian particles in a dense state.
key_observables: Density perturbation/wake shape, characteristic wake closing length ($\lambda$), and the density profile ($ho$).
important_parameters: Packing fraction ($\phi$), compressibility factor ($Z$), self-propulsion velocity ($v_p$), and persistence time ($	au_r$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on continuum descriptions, assuming the particle current is driven by pressure gradients against friction, and fitting the wake decay with an exponential function.
figures_summary: Figures show experimental setups, time-averaged density maps illustrating the wake, and quantitative plots demonstrating the non-monotonic dependence of wake length on density for both passive and active cases.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem by reviewing the wake formation. It then analyzes the passive case, identifying two density regimes governed by compressibility. Finally, it extends this understanding to active suspensions, quantifying the role of self-propulsion.
why_interesting: While focused on classical soft matter, the concepts of non-equilibrium steady states, effective interactions due to activity, and density fluctuations in confined/driven systems are highly relevant to understanding many-body dynamics in quantum many-body systems.

Figure 2 displays typical snapshots of a moving obstacle in a passive sediment. At all considered experimental condi- tions, we observe a density wake with an almost empty zone behind the obstacle. However, the length of this wake changes by about two orders of magnitude in units of the particle size.
